Replay

Replay checkpoint and recovery contract

8 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Data boundaryAPI and ownershipWire/file formatGodot persistenceInitial archive and save verificationOriginal M5 implementation sequence

A Replay authority archive lets a fresh process restore the World, player reservations, room rules, and action frontiers from a checkpoint. Recovery combines that state with an authorized successor, a newer authority epoch, and a handshake that reconciles surviving clients. An archive alone does not elect an authority or recover work accepted after its capture tick.

The implementation includes bounded replication to an explicitly trusted peer, authenticated coordinator RPCs with SQLite storage, durable provisioning, checkpoint publication, and cold restore. Native and browser gates cover planned and crash handoff, old-owner return, repeated handoff, control partition, and successor loss. The framework audit records the evidence and remaining deployment/recovery limits.

The explicit protocol-6 to 7 archive bridge preserves compatible Worlds while validating the old contract. It grants no new lease; coordinated upgrade remains an application transition. Normal loaders continue to reject incompatible versions.

Data boundary#

net.Checkpoint(State, Control, Action, Seats) owns:

Section Restored meaning
Version/contract Archive version, network protocol, schema/content contract, tick rate
Authority frame Exact tick and all state fields, including replay:"authority" fields
Configuration History, lead/prediction limits, timing, packet and traffic limits
Authority identity Previous epoch and generation counter; restore requires a newer epoch
Roster Stable seats, spectator/local status, token digests, connection-generation/serial counters
Membership decisions Pending join/leave/fresh-occupant masks and held controls
Action ledger Per-peer received/settled sequences, accepted queues, recent settled outcomes
Input buffer Accepted future input samples still relevant at the capture tick
Room policy Lock, banned credential digests, custom policy ID and bounded policy bytes

Entity IDs, pool generations, RNG, inventories, scheduled spawns, cooldowns, AI phase, ownership versions, and game progression are restored because they live in the complete authority frame. Game-specific state outside that frame is not implicitly captured. Immutable definitions are selected by the application and gated by content/schema identity.

An archive contains authority-only information and must only be disclosed to a trusted successor. Public client snapshots are a separate codec projection. Bearer reconnect tokens are not archived: the roster contains SHA-256 digests. The Godot profile file retains the player's actual token separately.

Runtime connections, allocators, callback addresses, transport queues, wall-clock timestamps, delta baselines, frame/event histories, and presentation journals are not serialized. Restore constructs fresh owners at stable addresses. There is no committed external-effect outbox implementation yet; do not use this archive as an exactly-once ledger for payments, achievements, or other persistent services.

API and ownership#

For an already initialized authority:

Odin
checkpoint: net.Checkpoint(World, Control, Action, SEATS)
defer net.checkpoint_destroy(&checkpoint)
error := net.checkpoint_capture(&server, &checkpoint)
// Check error before continuing.
bytes, encode_error := net.checkpoint_encode(&checkpoint, model)
defer delete(bytes)

Low-level listen hosts first install their local credential with server_set_local_token. Godot's session_open handles this. A custom admission callback requires a nonzero policy ID when capturing; callers supply its immutable serialized policy data. Restore requires the same policy ID and an explicitly reinstalled callback/user descriptor. Callback addresses are never decoded.

For restore, decode into an empty checkpoint with the application's expected content ID, then call server_restore into an uninitialized server. The two owned objects must not be shallow-copied. Destroy a checkpoint once, including after a failed read; decode failure leaves an empty destination, and decoding into an existing owner returns Wrong_Phase without modifying it. server_restore never overwrites an initialized server.

Resume_Options makes recovery decisions explicit:

  • epoch must be strictly newer than the archive epoch. Packet envelopes use it to reject delayed old-authority traffic. It does not itself establish legitimate leadership or prevent another process from continuing independently.
  • local_seat is zero for a dedicated authority or an existing playable seat for the new listen host. The Godot facade verifies its profile token against that reservation. Promoting a guest preserves their previous action sequence.
  • preserve_pending=true retains accepted action values, sequence IDs, scheduling, and rejection reasons. The caller must choose an appropriate membership policy and resume schedule. false explicitly settles those actions as Disconnected on subsequent ticks, preserving their IDs and the action frontier.
  • retain_membership=true preserves simulation membership while the migration driver pauses for peer recovery. Transport bindings still begin disconnected; the driver must enforce its pause/deadline policy. With false, formerly active remote seats leave on the first resumed tick. Rejoining before that tick replaces the pending leave. A reservation reconnect does not run fresh-player reset.

Accepted control samples can be retained with pending work, but input streams from old connections are retired on reconnect. The promoted seat resumes local device sampling; archived remote samples cannot override its new local input. Complete replay of every input after a crash requires a separate accepted-decision log.

Already executed gameplay is in the frame. Recent verdicts and settled/received frontiers prevent accepted sequence IDs from being applied again. Lost work after the archive tick is outside this guarantee. A surviving client that observed such work needs the recovery handshake to reconcile its newer frontier; changing its epoch is not a complete abrupt-recovery protocol.

Wire/file format#

Archive version 4 uses the canonical RPLY envelope (52 bytes), custom message kind 0x434b, and a fingerprint of the ordered section schemas. Network protocol version 7 and the complete runtime contract are checked inside the body. The body contains header, settings, authority frame, held controls/view contexts, sparse roster/actions/ inputs/outcomes/bans, and opaque policy bytes, in that order.

Limits include 1 MiB total archive, 16 peer records, 16 queued actions and 16 recent outcomes per peer, 64 bans, and 64 KiB of custom policy bytes. Future inputs are bounded by the restored configuration and exact body length. Header/configuration and all section sizes are checked before count-driven allocation. Field codecs validate canonical booleans/enums/finite floats; semantic checks validate unique seats, credential digests, action frontiers, scheduling, and outcome order. A malformed/truncated/oversized/wrong-content archive cannot partially install a world. The checksum detects accidental corruption; it is not authentication.

Schema/content/version mismatches currently reject the archive. There is no automatic schema upgrade. Converters must explicitly decode an old schema, convert the complete frame/session contract, validate the new result, and retain the old file until a new archive has been successfully written.

The archive can exceed the 64 KiB transport packet limit. The recovery transfer chunks it, bounds reassembly, verifies the complete archive, and acknowledges an archive identity before considering it usable. A packet send is not a durability acknowledgement.

Godot persistence#

session_save captures the authority and writes the archive. checkpoint_read reads and validates it; session_resume opens a fresh authority with explicit resume options. session_profile loads/creates a local credential and fails on an unreadable or malformed existing file. Use distinct profile paths for simultaneous players on the same machine.

The file adapter writes <path>.pending, checks the write/length/error, flushes and closes it, then renames it onto the destination. A later interrupted staging write does not replace a completed archive. This follows Godot's FileAccess flush/close and DirAccess replacement APIs. The adapter assumes one writer per path and an existing parent directory. The tested boundary is process crash/restart on native macOS. Power-loss durability, directory fsync behavior, concurrent writers, and browser persistence are not established by these tests.

Initial archive and save verification#

Shell
nix develop --command bash tests/replay_net/run.sh
nix develop --command bash examples/replay_cavecrawl/save_run.sh
nix develop --command bash examples/replay_cavecrawl/recovery_run.sh

The initial runner gate recorded 24 native tests with allocator tracking and an instantiated WASM type-check. Seven checkpoint scenarios cover canonical roundtrip, hidden authority fields, promotion, pending actions, malformed/count/content/contract failures, policy and ban restoration, new-epoch rejection, and fresh clients reclaiming reserved seats without resetting loot. A local host credential cannot reserve a second remote seat.

The solo Godot gate creates/replaces a save after looting, opening a door, and throwing a rock; leaves a deliberately incomplete staging file; kills the writer; and starts a fresh process using the saved profile. The entire restored frame's canonical hash/tick match, and the next action succeeds without repeating old outcomes. The co-op gate runs a host and guest at 120 ms receive delay each, saves the guest's looted world, kills/replaces the processes, and checks guest identity, inventory conservation, door state, and continued actions under epoch 2. It supplies the new epoch explicitly. These gates are registered in tests/run_all.sh.

Original M5 implementation sequence#

This sequence records the work planned after the initial archive/save gates. The implementation and test counts below describe that stage.

  1. Bounded checkpoint transfer — implemented component: explicit trusted-peer scope, indexed chunks, duplicate/reorder handling, complete validation, acknowledgement, and retention of the authority's last acknowledged checkpoint now pass eight native tests and a real ENet large-archive gate. See the replication package. Integration with gameplay packet routing/traffic budgets and reusable archive schema metadata now also exists as recovery.Link and the Godot Session facade. A live Cavecrawl gate validates gameplay and repeated backups on one connection under network faults.
  2. Authority decision service — implemented component: the authority package defines durable CAS decisions, eligible successors, conservative leases, planned retirement, restart quarantine, and runner enforcement. Authenticated RPCs and SQLite storage now have real-process handoff and coordinator crash/restart gates. The test transfers the simulation. The Room driver additionally passes live Cavecrawl client migration; dynamic provisioning and the full failure matrix remain open. Dedicated competitive failover stays within trusted infrastructure.
  3. Recovery handshake: coordinator-approved authority/epoch discovery, reconnect retries, old/new frontier reconciliation, deliberate retirement of unreplicated actions, and local presentation reset/cancellation at the recovered tick.
  4. Planned handoff: freeze admission at a final tick/frontier, replicate and acknowledge that checkpoint, authorize the successor, reconnect, and resume. Verify no accepted work is omitted and old authority packets remain rejected.
  5. Abrupt takeover: restore the newest acknowledged eligible checkpoint, explicitly report the lost tick interval, handle successor failure/consecutive migrations/old-host return, and keep divergent partitions from silently merging.
  6. Gameplay acceptance: real-process kills during Cavecrawl combat and loot, then a competitive replayed example. Record interruption, rollback distance, checkpoint age and size, restore cost, and responsiveness after recovery.

The initial sequence deferred checkpoint-plus-log recovery, service outboxes, and broader schema upgrades until after snapshot-based acceptance. It left M5 open until the driver, fencing, partition policy, and real successor takeover gates existed. The framework audit records the later implemented recovery paths and their remaining limits.
